title: Breadboard week one: LED and button
summary: Two weeks: light an LED from a micro:bit pin through a resistor you choose yourself on a real breadboard, then wire a button as real input.

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan
steps.body:
The design loop again: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix. This week the circuit lives outside the micro:bit, on a breadboard, and that changes what can go wrong.

Ask: what do you want to build? A light you switch on from code, through a real wire, a real resistor and a real LED. Then a button your code can actually read.

Imagine before you build. Sketch the loop on paper: a line out of pin 0, through the resistor, into the LED, and back to GND. A loop is a full circle that ends where it started. If your drawing does not close, the real circuit will not either.

Plan the pieces:

1. The micro:bit clips onto the edge connector breakout board, so its tiny edge pins can reach a breadboard hole.
2. Pin 0, a wire, the resistor and the LED make one loop back to GND.
3. The button is a second loop later, from a different pin to GND.

This week runs over two weeks. The first ends when the LED lights; a step called Good place to stop marks it.

figure.alt: A current loop drawn as four labeled boxes joined by arrows going one way around: P0, where the current starts, into the resistor labeled 330 ohms or more, into the LED, which only conducts from anode to cathode, and back to GND, where the current returns, closing the loop back at P0.

items.s: LED backwards: no current, no light
330 ohm holds the current near 3 mA

steps.title: Current, resistance and the loop
steps.body:
Current is electricity on the move: the amount of charge flowing past a point every second, the way a river's current is water moving past a rock. A wire gives it a path, the way a pipe gives water a path.

A resistor resists: it slows the current down. An LED cannot take much current, and neither can a micro:bit pin. With no resistor, too much would rush through and burn out the LED's tiny glowing chip, or damage the pin. 330 ohms holds the current to about 3 thousandths of an amp: plenty to light the LED, nowhere near enough to hurt it. The next step shows you how to work that number out.

You met this in week 1: an LED is a one-way valve. Current flows only from its longer leg to its shorter leg. Put it in backwards and nothing lights at all, not even a flicker. That is not a broken LED; turn it around.

The circuit only works as one unbroken loop: pin 0, the resistor, the LED, back to GND. Code can have one wrong block and mostly work. A circuit cannot: one wire a single hole off breaks the whole loop, and nothing lights anywhere on it.

steps.title: Choosing your own resistor
steps.body:
Ohm's law links push, flow and resistance: R = V / I. R is resistance in ohms, V is the push in volts, I is the current in amps.

Every part in the loop uses up some of the push: the LED about 2 volts of it, and the resistor the rest.

Work out your own resistor:

1. The pin pushes with about 3 volts.
2. A red LED uses about 2 of them, which leaves about 1 volt for the resistor.
3. You want about 3 milliamps, which is 3 thousandths of an amp.
4. 1 volt divided by 3 thousandths is the same as 1,000 divided by 3: about 333 ohms.
5. The nearest size sold is 330 ohms.

Check it backwards: 1,000 divided by 330 is about 3, so about 3 milliamps.

330 ohms is also the floor: never go below it. A micro:bit pin can safely give only about 5 milliamps, and 330 ohms keeps it near 4, even on USB, where the pin pushes nearer 3.3 volts and leaves 1.3 for the resistor.

Bigger is allowed. 470 or 1,000 ohms lets less current through, and the LED glows dimmer.

steps.title: How a breadboard is joined inside

figure.alt: A breadboard seen from above. Along the top edge run two separate rails, a + rail and a - rail, each joined along its own length; two more run along the bottom edge. Between them, four columns numbered 6 to 9 are each drawn as two tall strips: an upper strip for holes a to e and a lower strip for holes f to j. The strips for column 6 are shaded. A gap runs across the middle, labeled center gap, top and bottom not joined. Small text says columns are not joined to each other, and beside each strip that 5 holes are joined.

items.s: columns are not joined to each other
center gap: top and bottom not joined

steps.body:
Under the plastic, metal strips join some holes and keep others apart.

1. Each numbered column is two strips of five holes: a to e are joined, and f to j are joined.
2. The center gap splits them: a6 is not joined to f6.
3. Two different columns are never joined, unless you add a wire or a part between them.
4. Along each long edge run two rails, one marked + and one marked -. Each rail is joined along its own length, but the + rail and the - rail are never joined to each other. On some full-size boards each rail is split in the middle; a break in its printed red or blue line shows where.

So a part's two legs must sit in two different strips, or the current slips along the metal and skips the part. That is why your resistor goes from column 6 to column 9.

figure.alt: A wiring diagram of the LED breadboard circuit. The edge connector breakout's P0 pin wires to hole a6, a 330-ohm-or-higher resistor bridges column 6 to column 9 in row c, the LED sits in row a from column 9 (anode) to column 10 (cathode), and a wire runs from hole c10 back to the breakout's GND pin, closing the loop.

items.s: P0, resistor, LED, GND: one loop

steps.title: Wire the LED and light it
steps.body:
Getting ready:

1. The micro:bit clips into the edge connector breakout board so it can reach the breadboard.
2. Holes in rows a to e of the same column are already connected to each other.
3. Never choose a resistor below 330 ohms. Bigger is fine, like 470 or 1,000 ohms, and gives a dimmer LED.
4. A wire from a breakout pin starts in a free hole in the same column as that pin's leg, or on the pin itself if the breakout sits off the breadboard.
5. Use a red LED. A red one needs only about 2 volts, so it lights well from the pin's 3; a blue or white one needs nearly all 3 and may barely glow.

Wire the LED:

1. Push the micro:bit into the edge connector breakout board, gold pins first, until it sits snug.
2. On a full-size breadboard, push the breakout's legs in at the far end, column 35 or higher, straddling the center gap. Your circuit uses columns 6 to 20, and a leg in the same column as a part is joined to that part's strip. On a small breadboard, keep the breakout off the board and connect it with jumper wires, like the picture.
3. Run a jumper wire from the pin labeled `0` on the breakout board to hole a6.
4. Leave a second jumper wire ready near a `GND` pin, for the last step.
5. Find the colored stripes or the printed number on each resistor in your kit.
6. Predict first: how many milliamps would a 1,000 ohm resistor let through? Work it out the way Choosing your own resistor did, and write your number down.
7. Bend a resistor of 330 ohms or higher into a wide U shape.
8. Push one resistor leg into hole c6, the same column as your `0` wire.
9. Push the other resistor leg into hole c9.
10. Find the LED's long leg, the anode, and its short leg, next to the flat side.
11. Push the LED's long leg into hole a9, the same column as the resistor's second leg.
12. Push the LED's short leg into hole a10, the column next to it.
13. Run your last jumper wire from hole c10 to a `GND` pin on the breakout board.
14. If you have a bigger resistor, like 470 or 1,000 ohms, swap it in and compare the brightness. A 1,000 ohm one checks your step 6 number: at about a third of the current, the LED should look clearly dimmer. No 1,000 ohm resistor? Check your step 6 number on paper instead: 1,000 divided by 1,000.

The loop is now complete: pin 0, the wire, the resistor, the LED, another wire, back to GND.

Light it up:

1. Open https://makecode.microbit.org and start a new project.
2. From `Basic`, drag an `on start` block onto the canvas.
3. From `Pins`, snap a `digital write pin` block inside `on start`, set to P0, value 1.
4. Press `Download` to send the program to your micro:bit over USB.
5. The LED should light up the moment the program runs and stay lit.
6. If nothing lights up, check every hole against this page before assuming it is broken.
7. If it still does not light up, check whether the LED is in backwards.
checklist: The LED lights up steady the moment the program runs
The resistor sits in the loop between P0 and the LED, not skipped
If nothing lit up, I checked whether the LED was in backwards before assuming it was broken
Every wire and leg sits in the exact hole this page named, not one hole off
I wrote down which resistor value I chose (330 ohms or higher) and what I noticed about its brightness

steps.title: Good place to stop
steps.body:
Your LED lights from your own code, so this is the end of week one of this quest; the rest is next week.

Before you stop:

1. Unclip the battery pack and unplug the USB cable.
2. Leave the micro:bit in the breakout, and every wire, the resistor and the LED, exactly where they are.
3. Set the breadboard somewhere flat where nothing can knock a wire loose.
4. Write in the Maker's Log which resistor you chose and what you noticed about its brightness.

Week two starts at the next step, Why 0 means pressed, and then the button.

When you come back, plug the USB cable in first. Your program stays on the micro:bit, so the LED should light by itself. If it does not, a wire moved: check every hole against the wiring picture before you add anything new.

steps.title: Why 0 means pressed
steps.body:
In the next step your code checks `digital read pin P1 = 0` to mean the button is pressed. That looks backwards, so here is why.

A pin used as an input reads the push, the voltage, on it: near 3 volts reads 1, near 0 volts reads 0. A pin joined to nothing has no steady push at all. It floats, and a floating pin can read 1, then 0, then 1 again, just from your hand coming near.

The `set pull pin P1 to up` block fixes that. Inside the chip it joins P1 to 3 volts through a big resistor, about 13,000 ohms, around forty times your 330. With the button loose, that gentle pull holds P1 at about 3 volts, so it reads 1.

Press the button and P1 joins GND straight through the button's metal, with almost no resistance at all. GND wins, P1 drops to 0 volts, and it reads 0.

Loose reads 1, pressed reads 0. Engineers call this a pull-up.

figure.alt: A wiring diagram of the button added across the breadboard's center gap. A button straddles the gap with legs in row e (top half) and row f (bottom half). A wire runs from the breakout's P1 pin to row e, and a wire from GND to row f. Text notes that P1 is pulled up, so it reads 1 loose and 0 pressed, and repeats two safety lines: unclip the battery before moving wires, and never bridge 3V straight to GND.

items.s: unclip the battery before moving wires
never bridge 3V straight to GND: short circuit

steps.title: Add the button
steps.body:
Getting ready:

1. The LED circuit from the last step stays wired exactly as it was.
2. Unclip the battery pack before you move any wires, so your hands are never inside a live circuit.

Wire the button:

1. Push a push button across the breadboard's center gap, a few columns over from the LED.
2. Land two of its legs in row e and two in row f, straddling the gap.
3. Run a jumper wire from the pin labeled `1` on the breakout board to a hole in row e.
4. Land that wire in the same column as one of the button's legs.
5. Run another jumper wire from any `GND` pin to a hole in row f.
6. Use the column where a leg on the other side of the gap landed.

Pressing the button joins those two sides together; letting go separates them again.

Build the code:

1. Open your project in https://makecode.microbit.org.
2. From the `Pins` `Advanced` drawer, drag a `set pull pin` block onto `on start`, set to P1, pull up.
3. Delete the `digital write pin` block from the last step.
4. From `Basic`, drag a `forever` block onto the canvas.
5. From `Logic`, drag an `if then else` block inside `forever`.
6. Build the check `digital read pin P1 = 0`, using an `=` block from `Logic`.
7. Inside the `if` branch, snap in `digital write pin P0 to 1`.
8. Inside the `else` branch, snap in `digital write pin P0 to 0`.

Run it on the board:

1. Press `Download` to send the program to your micro:bit over USB.
2. The LED should stay dark until you press the button.
3. It should light up for as long as you hold the button, and go dark when you let go.

Safety: 3V and `GND` on the micro:bit are both safe to touch. Never wire 3V straight to `GND` with nothing in between; that is a short circuit.
checklist: The LED is off until I press the button, and on while I hold it down
The button straddles the center gap of the breadboard, not sitting on one side only
The two wires to the button are on opposite sides of the gap, not the same side
I unclipped the battery before moving any wires

steps.title: What a volt measures
steps.body:
Current is the flow: how much charge moves past a point every second, like water in a river moving past a rock. But water only flows if something pushes it. A river runs because its water starts high up a hill and runs down to the sea.

Voltage is that push. It is measured in volts, written V, and it always compares two points, the way a hill has a top and a bottom. That is why a multimeter has two probes: it reads the push between wherever you touch them.

Your micro:bit's pin 0, switched on, pushes with about 3 volts compared with GND. Every part in the loop uses up some of that push, the way a river drops a little at every waterfall. The LED uses about 2 volts just to light. The resistor uses up the rest.

No push, no flow. The extra Measure the resistor's narrowing puts a multimeter on exactly this.

steps.title: Bug diary
steps.body: Write one line for each thing that did not work the first time and what you tried. If the LED never lit at all, say which of the two classic breadboard mistakes it turned out to be: a wire in the wrong hole, or the LED in backwards. If the button did not change anything, check that its two wires really are on opposite sides of the center gap, not the same side. If you compared two resistor values, say which one you kept and why.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photo of the breadboard circuit running, and paste the MakeCode share link or the JavaScript from the editor

extras.title: Make the LED blink instead of glow steady
extras.body:
Turn the steady LED into a blinking one, using only code.

1. Open your project at https://makecode.microbit.org.
2. Keep the wiring you already built: pin 0, the resistor, the LED, and back to GND.
3. Inside your `forever` block, delete the `if then else` block that reads the button.
4. Inside `forever`, snap `digital write pin P0 to 1`, then a `pause (ms)` block.
5. Type a number into `pause (ms)`, then snap `digital write pin P0 to 0` and another `pause (ms)` with the same number.
6. Press `Download` and watch the LED blink.

What to notice: below about 20 milliseconds per step, the blink looks steady again, the same trick from week one's screen.

extras.title: Hold for fast, let go for slow
extras.body:
Make the button change how fast the LED blinks, instead of only turning it on and off.

1. Keep the button wired the way you built it, on pin 1 with `set pull pin` set to pull up.
2. From `Variables`, make a new variable called `blinkTime` and set it to 400 in `on start`.
3. From `Logic`, drag an `if then else` block inside your `forever` loop.
4. Build the check `digital read pin P1 = 0`, using an `=` block from `Logic`.
5. In the `if` branch, snap `set blinkTime to 100`.
6. In the `else` branch, snap `set blinkTime to 400`.
7. Below the `if then else`, snap `digital write pin P0 to 1`, then a `pause (ms)` block using `blinkTime`.
8. After that, snap `digital write pin P0 to 0`, then another `pause (ms)` block using `blinkTime`.
9. Press `Download` and compare the blink held down against the blink let go.

What to notice: the LED reads the button fresh every trip through the loop, so it can change speed mid-blink.

extras.title: Design your own signal
extras.body:
What could a single LED and a single button tell someone, without any words on a screen?

Design one new signal using the LED and button you wired this week.

It must use the button you wired this week.
It must have one number you choose by testing, like a pause or a count.
It must be shown to someone in your house, working on the real breadboard.

Sketch your signal on paper before you touch the breadboard.

How to know it works: someone who has never seen it can guess what it means after watching once.

extras.title: Measure the resistor's narrowing
extras.body:
Find out how the resistor and the LED share the same voltage between them.

1. Predict first: guess how many volts the multimeter will read across just the LED. Write your number in the Maker's Log.
2. Set a multimeter to measure DC volts.
3. With your circuit built and lit, touch the two probes across the LED's two legs and read the number.
4. Now touch the two probes across the resistor's two legs and read that number too.
5. Add the two readings together in the Maker's Log.

Compare: was your prediction close to the LED's real reading, and do the two readings together roughly match the voltage your circuit gets?

Teach it: tell a grown-up in two sentences why the resistor and the LED share the voltage instead of the LED getting all of it.

extras.title: Wire a second LED
extras.body:
Find out whether a second LED on its own path steals any of the push from the first path.

1. Predict first: how many volts will you read across the whole first path, from column 6 to column 10, once the second LED is lit? Write your number in the Maker's Log.
2. Unclip the battery pack and unplug the USB cable.
3. Move the breakout end of the wire from `0` over to the breakout's `3V` pin, so both paths get their push from the board's supply instead of asking one pin for double the current.
4. Plug the USB cable back in. The first LED lights with no code at all.
5. Set the multimeter to DC volts. Touch one probe to the resistor's leg in c6 and the other to the LED's short leg in a10, and write down that whole-path reading. Then measure across just the LED's two legs.
6. Unplug the USB cable again.
7. Push a jumper wire from hole d6 to hole a16, so column 16 shares the push from column 6.
8. Push a second resistor, 330 ohms or higher, from hole c16 to hole c19.
9. Push a second red LED's long leg into hole a19 and its short leg into hole a20.
10. Run a jumper wire from hole c20 to hole d10, the column already joined to GND.
11. Plug the USB cable back in. Both LEDs should light.
12. Measure the whole first path again, c6 to a10, then the whole second path, c16 to a20, and write down both readings.
13. When you finish, unplug, take out the second path, and move the wire from `3V` back to `0`.

If your button sits anywhere in columns 16 to 20, move columns 16, 19 and 20 further right onto empty columns. Keep d6 and d10 exactly where they are: they join the new path to 3V and to GND.

Your first LED and its resistor are in series: one path, the same current through both. The second path is in parallel with the first: side by side, each path getting the whole push, about 3 volts on batteries and about 3.3 on USB, which its resistor and LED then share. Each LED gets its own resistor, because no two LEDs are exactly alike, and two sharing one resistor let one hog the current. `3V` through a resistor and an LED is safe; `3V` straight to `GND` is still a short circuit.

Compare: did the whole-path reading change when the second LED lit, and how close was your number?

Teach it: tell a grown-up in two sentences why each path in parallel gets the whole push instead of half of it.
